name: Intel Gaudi 3 (HL-325 OAM / HL-338 PCIe)
memory_bandwidth_basis: Vendor-published per-accelerator figure from the Gaudi 3 technical paper: 128 GB HBM2e across 8 chips and 3.7 TB/s of HBM bandwidth.
notes: Two compute dies on an interposer bridge, presented to software as one unified die: 8 MME engines, 64 TPC engines and 24x 200 Gbps RDMA NIC ports in total. The published BF16 and FP8 MME TFLOPS are IDENTICAL at 1678, which is unusual and worth not misreading as a typo: Intel's paper reports both matrix engines at that figure, and separately quotes BF16 VECTOR TFLOPS at 28.7. Dense/sparse is not stated in the paper, so both rows are marked dense on the vendor's own framing. TDP is not published in the technical paper. THE HIERARCHY POINT: unlike the SRAM-only parts, Gaudi 3 has a real memory hierarchy with a meaningful SRAM tier between HBM and compute - 96 MB on-die (double Gaudi 2's 48 MB) at 12.8/6.4 TB/s read/write - which is what lets it run batch-1 decode with less pure HBM traffic than its compute peak would suggest. At 3.7 TB/s and 128 GB it sits at 453 FLOP/byte BF16, so it is memory-bound at batch 1 but far less severely than a 3-4x faster compute part would be. Ethernet-first scaling is the strategic point: 1200 GB/s bidirectional of RoCE versus H100's 900 GB/s of closed NVLink, and 24 200G NICs per part versus H100's 18. That trades a software problem (collectives over standard Ethernet) for avoiding proprietary fabric lock-in. Ships as OAM HL-325/HL-325L, PCIe HL-338, and the HLB-325 baseboard.
